newsitem.title: FRANCE: It's the "Boris Yeltsin Show" at NATO-Russia meet.
newsitem.headline: It's the "Boris Yeltsin Show" at NATO-Russia meet.

text.p: It was the "Boris Yeltsin Show" at Tuesday's NATO-Russia summit in Paris, with the Kremlin chief putting on an impromptu performance which caught even his own delegation off guard.
Showing few signs of the health problems which sidelined him for eight months until February, the 66-year-old Russian president was at his most playful and unpredictable.
Never one to stand on protocol, Yeltsin -- who had just signed a Russia-NATO partnership accord -- returned to the podium for a second, unscheduled speech to announce an unexpected arms proposal.
Puzzled U.S. officials sought an explanation, the stunned Russian delegation flew into a panic.

Only later did a spokesman clarify Yeltsin's comments. Although the Kremlin chief had said Moscow would remove the warheads from all missiles targeted at NATO states, what he had meant to say was that the missiles would be retargeted away from those countries.
"I think, judging by everything, this initiative was triggered by the atmosphere of goodwill and welcome which dominates the summit," presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said.
Yeltsin seemed genuinely to be having a good time.
When it came to his turn to sign the historic accord setting out relations with NATO, he gave a deep, theatrical sigh as if hesitating to put his name to the agreement.
Then he suddenly broke into a broad grin, made swivelling movements with the pen as if burying it into the paper and tapped the top for good measure.
Yeltsin also enjoyed the irony of his younger U.S. counterpart, Bill Clinton, having to use a walking stick after a fall.

Yeltsin, whose ability to rule was questioned at home and abroad after he had heart surgery last November and then suffered a bout of pneumonia, handed Clinton the cane with a rueful grin as the U.S. president got up to speak.

The Kremlin leader did not always seem at his best. Arriving at the Elysee Palace in Paris for the signing ceremony, he waved to photographers but then started moving slowly towards a guard of honour before French President Jacques Chirac ushered him carefully into the palace.

He also moved stiffly and looked awkward when NATO Secretary General Javier Solana embraced him after the signing ceremony, apparently unaware how many times he was expected to exchange kisses on the cheek.
It was not quite the back-slapping performance Yeltsin put on at a summit with Clinton in autumn 1995, when he had the U.S. president doubled up in laughter after poking fun at reporters.
But Yeltsin appealed relaxed again after his battle with ill health, reviving memories of some of his more unpredictable performances.

Notable among these was the time, after a champagne lunch, when he seized the baton from a conductor and conducted a police marching band at a ceremony in Germany in August 1994 marking the departure of former Soviet troops.
In September 1994, he failed to get off his plane at Shannon airport after a flight from the United States, leaving the Irish prime minister waiting in vain for him to emerge.
